title: Equations about rates
objectives: Write a differential equation from a story about a rate, and check a proposed solution.

screens.title: Growing at 5% of itself
screens.prose: £1,000 sits in an account. At every moment it grows at 5% of itself a year, so its slope is $0.05B$. Pick a candidate curve, drag the point along it and compare the tangent's slope with $0.05B$ in the caption.

derive.caption: At $t$ = {{fixed(p1.x, 1)}} the balance is {{money(p1.y)}}, so $0.05B$ = {{fixed(0.05 * p1.y, 1)}}.

screens.question: Which candidate has slope equal to $0.05B$ at every point?

options.why: You matched the slope at $t = 0$, where 50 is $0.05 \times 1000$. Later the line's slope stays 50 while $0.05B$ grows.
You took yearly compounding. Its slope is $\ln(1.05)B \approx 0.0488B$, a little short of $0.05B$ everywhere.

feedback.correct: The continuous curve keeps its slope at exactly $0.05B$ wherever the point sits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag the point to $t = 8$ on each candidate and compare the two numbers.

explain.text: Only $B = 1000e^{0.05t}$ has slope $0.05B$ at every $t$. The line matches at the start and then falls behind. Yearly steps grow at $\ln 1.05 \approx 4.88\%$, not 5%.

screens.title: An equation about a rate
screens.prose: What we just matched is a **differential equation**: $\dfrac{dB}{dt} = 0.05B$, with $B(0) = 1000$. Its solution is the function $B(t) = 1000e^{0.05t}$, whose slope is $0.05 \times 1000e^{0.05t} = 0.05B$.
screens.question: What is the balance after one year, to the penny?

hints.text: The solution is a function of $t$.

byKey.yearly: You paid 5% once at the year end. Continuous growth earns interest on the interest all year: £1,051.27.
byKey.ten: That is the ten-year balance on the chart. Put $t = 1$, not $t = 10$.

explain.text: $B(1) = 1000e^{0.05} = \text{£}1{,}051.27$, and $B(10) = 1000e^{0.5} = \text{£}1{,}648.72$. The extra £1.27 in the first year is interest earned on interest.

screens.title: Checking a solution
screens.prose: A solution is a function, not a number. To check $y = 3e^{2t}$ in $y' = 2y$, differentiate and substitute. Drag the point and compare the slope with $2y$.
screens.question: What happens when we substitute $y = 3e^{2t}$?

options.text: $y' = 6e^{2t}$, which equals $2y$ for every $t$, so it is a solution
$y' = 3e^{2t}$, which is half of $2y$, so it fails
options.why: You dropped the chain rule. The derivative of $e^{2t}$ is $2e^{2t}$.
You checked a starting value, which says nothing about $y'$. A solution must satisfy the equation at every $t$.
You treated the exponent like a power of $t$. The rule is $(e^{kt})' = ke^{kt}$.

hints.text: Compare $6e^{2t}$ with $2y = 6e^{2t}$: they agree for every $t$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate $3e^{2t}$ with the chain rule, then compare with $2y$.

byKey.chain: You dropped the factor 2 from the chain rule. $(3e^{2t})' = 6e^{2t}$.

explain.text: $y' = 6e^{2t}$ and $2y = 6e^{2t}$, so the two sides agree for every $t$. The slope on the chart equals $2y$ wherever we drag.

screens.title: One value picks the curve
screens.prose: Every $y = Ce^{0.5t}$ solves $y' = 0.5y$, so the equation alone gives a whole family. One known value picks the member. We know $y(2) = 5.44$.
screens.question: Slide $C$ until the curve passes through the marked point.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the caption's $y(2)$ and stop at 5.44.

explain.text: $y(2) = Ce^{1}$, so $C = 5.4366/e = 2$. Then $C$ is also $y(0)$, the starting value.

screens.title: From a story to an equation
screens.prose: A £100,000 loan accrues interest at 6% a year, continuously. The borrower repays £12,000 a year, spread evenly. Interest adds $0.06L$ a year and repayments take £12,000 a year away.
screens.question: Which equation describes the balance $L(t)$?

options.why: You added the repayment. Repaying lowers the balance, so it enters with a minus sign.
You wrote the rate on its own. Interest is 6% **of the balance**, so it is $0.06L$.
You made interest shrink the loan. Interest adds to what is owed.

hints.text: What adds to the loan, and what takes away?

feedback.correct: Rate of change = interest in minus repayments out: $L' = 0.06L - 12000$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the rate of change as what flows in minus what flows out.

explain.text: Each year interest adds $0.06L$ and repayments remove 12,000, so $L' = 0.06L - 12000$. The curve shows the balance falling to zero after about 11.6 years; lesson 3 solves it.

screens.title: A rate pulled to a level
screens.prose: A short rate is pulled towards 4% at speed 0.5: $r' = 0.5(0.04 - r)$. The further it sits from 4%, the faster it moves. Today it is 6%.
screens.question: What is $r'$ today, in rate per year?

feedback.correct: $0.5(0.04 - 0.06) = -0.01$: the rate falls by about 1 point a year at first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $r = 0.06$ into $0.5(0.04 - r)$.

byKey.sign: You took $r - 0.04$. Above 4% the pull is downwards, so $r'$ is negative.
byKey.gap: You kept the gap, $-0.02$, and dropped the speed 0.5.

explain.text: $r' = 0.5(0.04 - 0.06) = -0.01$, the slope of the tangent at the start. As the gap shrinks the slope flattens. Lesson 5 solves this equation.

screens.title: Order and linearity
screens.prose: The **order** is the highest derivative. An equation is **linear** when $y$ and its derivatives each appear alone, to the first power, times functions of $t$. No two of them are multiplied together. So $ty' + y = \sin t$ is linear, but $y' = y^2$ and $yy' = t$ are not.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which are linear and first-order?

options.why: You saw a first derivative only. $y^2$ is a power of $y$, so it is nonlinear.
$\sin y$ is a nonlinear function of $y$; $\sin t$ would be fine.
It is linear, but $y''$ makes it second-order. Level 2 treats these.

hints.text: Look for $y$ inside a power or a function.
$t^2y$ multiplies $y$ by a function of $t$, which is allowed.

feedback.correct: Three are linear first-order: $t^2y$ is fine because $t^2$ is only a coefficient.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check two things: the highest derivative, and whether $y$ appears inside a power or a function.

explain.text: $y' = 2y$, $L' = 0.06L - 12000$ and $y' = t^2y + e^t$ are linear first-order. $y^2$ and $\sin y$ are nonlinear in $y$. $y'' = -y$ is second-order.

screens.title: One point is not enough
screens.prose: A colleague checks $y = 1 + 2t$ in $y' = 2y$. At $t = 0$: $y = 1$ and $y' = 2 = 2y$. She calls it a solution. Drag the point along the line.
screens.question: Is $y = 1 + 2t$ a solution of $y' = 2y$?

options.text: No: at $t = 1$ the slope is 2 but $2y = 6$

options.why: You checked one point. The equation must hold at every $t$, and at $t = 1$ it fails.

options.text: Yes, because both sides are linear
options.why: Being linear says nothing about agreeing. The slope is always 2 while $2y$ grows.

options.text: Only for $t$ near 0, so it is an approximate solution
options.why: Close to $t = 0$ it is the tangent line, a good approximation. A solution must agree exactly everywhere.

hints.text: The slope of the line is always 2, so it fails at $t = 1$.

feedback.correct: At $t = 1$: $y' = 2$ but $2y = 6$. One matching point is not a solution.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag the point to $t = 1$ and compare the slope with $2y$.

byKey.yes: You checked only at $t = 0$. At $t = 1$ the slope is 2 and $2y$ is 6, so it fails.

explain.text: $y' = 2$ for every $t$, while $2y = 2 + 4t$. They agree only at $t = 0$, so this is the tangent line of the true solution $e^{2t}$ there.

screens.title: A residual check in NumPy
screens.prose: A computer checks a candidate the same way, at many points at once. The **residual** at $t$ is $|y'(t) - f(t, y(t))|$. Pass the functions in and evaluate on a whole array `ts`.
screens.question: Complete `residual` and `is_solution`.

widget.starter:

def residual(y, dy, rhs, ts):
    """Largest |y'(t) - rhs(t, y(t))| over the array ts."""
    ...

def is_solution(y, dy, rhs, ts, tol=1e-6):
    """True when the residual is at most tol."""
    ...

y = lambda t: 1 + 2*t; dy = lambda t: 2 + 0*t; rhs = lambda t, y: 2*y
y = lambda t: 1 + 2*t; dy = lambda t: 2 + 0*t; rhs = lambda t, y: 2*y

tests.call: residual(lambda t: np.exp(t), lambda t: np.exp(t), lambda t, y: 2*y, np.array([0, 1]))

tests.setup: y = lambda t: 3*np.exp(2*t); dy = lambda t: 6*np.exp(2*t); rhs = lambda t, y: 2*y
y = lambda t: 1 + 2*t; dy = lambda t: 2 + 0*t; rhs = lambda t, y: 2*y

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: residuals within 1e-9 (or a relative 1e-9), and two True or False checks. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: Work on arrays: `y(ts)` gives every value at once.
`dy(ts) - rhs(ts, y(ts))` is the array of residuals with signs.
`return float(np.max(np.abs(dy(ts) - rhs(ts, y(ts)))))`, and `is_solution` compares that with `tol`.

feedback.correct: The largest residual over the grid is the check; zero up to rounding means a solution.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Evaluate `dy(ts)` and `rhs(ts, y(ts))` as arrays, then take the largest absolute difference.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with a return statement.

NumPy evaluates the functions on the whole array, so one line gives every residual.

```python
return float(np.max(np.abs(dy(ts) - rhs(ts, y(ts)))))
```

screens.title: What a solution is
screens.prose:
A first-order equation sets the slope from the time and the value:

$$y' = f(t, y).$$

A **solution** is a function $y(t)$ with $y'(t) = f(t, y(t))$ at every $t$ in an interval. A starting value $y(0)$ picks one solution from the family, provided $f$ and its derivative in $y$ are continuous.
screens.question: Which function solves $y' = -3y$ with $y(0) = 2$?

options.why: You swapped the rate and the start. The rate goes in the exponent and the start in front.
You matched the value and slope at $t = 0$ only, as with $1 + 2t$ earlier.
This has $y(0) = 2$, but its slope is $-3e^{-3t}$, not $-3y$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check both the equation and the starting value for each candidate.

explain.text: $(2e^{-3t})' = -6e^{-3t} = -3(2e^{-3t})$, and at $t = 0$ it is 2. The other candidates fail the equation or the start.

screens.title: Compounding more often
screens.prose: A desk quotes rates continuously compounded. To see why, compound £1,000 at 5% more and more often for one year: $1000(1 + 0.05/n)^n$.
screens.question: Fill in the balance after one year for each frequency.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $1000(1 + 0.05/n)^n$ for each $n$, to the penny.

byKey.r1c2: Check the monthly row: raise $(1 + 0.05/12)$ to the 12th power, not times 12.
byKey.simple: You added 5% of £1000 once, which is simple interest. Compounding earns interest on interest each month.

ideas: A differential equation states a rate of change in terms of time and the value itself.
A solution is a function that satisfies the equation at every $t$. One starting value picks it from the family when $f$ is smooth.
Check a candidate by differentiating and substituting at every $t$, not at a single point.

formula.name: Exponential growth
formula.note: Compounding ever more often gives the same limit, so desks use $e^{-rT}$ to discount.

summary.trap: Matching the equation at $t = 0$ only: $1 + 2t$ fits $y' = 2y$ there and nowhere else.

quiz.prose: Coffee at 80°C sits in a room at 20°C. It cools at a rate proportional to the gap to the room.
quiz.question: Which equation fits, with $k > 0$?

options.why: You made the gap grow. A hot cup cools, so $T'$ is negative while $T > 20$.
You measured from 0°C. The coffee heads to the room's 20°C, not to 0.
You made it cool at a fixed speed. The rate depends on the gap.

feedback.correct: $T' = -k(T - 20)$: the gap shrinks at a rate proportional to itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the rate in terms of the gap $T - 20$.

explain.text: Cooling is proportional to the gap and makes $T$ fall while $T > 20$. So $T' = -k(T - 20)$, the same shape as the short rate's pull.

quiz.prose: The equation $y' = 2y$ has the family $y = Ce^{2t}$.
quiz.question: Which constant value $c$ makes $y(t) = c$ a solution?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A constant has slope 0, so we need $2c = 0$.

byKey.two: The 2 is the growth rate, not a value. $2y = 4$ there.

explain.text: A constant has $y' = 0$, so it solves $y' = 2y$ only when $2c = 0$, so $c = 0$. It is the member $C = 0$ of the family, an equilibrium.

quiz.prose: A desk discounts at a continuously compounded 4% a year.
quiz.question: What is the discount factor for a payment in five years?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The factor is $e^{-rT}$.

byKey.yearly: You used $1.04^{-5}$, yearly compounding. The desk's rate is continuous.

explain.text: $D = e^{-rT} = e^{-0.2} = 0.8187$, so £100 in five years is worth £81.87 today.

feedback.correct: The highest derivative is $y''$, so the order is 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the highest derivative.

byKey.one: You counted the $y'$ term. $y''$ is higher.
byKey.three: The 3 is a coefficient, not a derivative.

explain.text: Order is the highest derivative that appears, here $y''$: order 2. It is also linear.
